title: Find the Duplicate Number
keyIdea: Draw an arrow i → nums[i]. The array becomes a road leading into a loop, and the duplicate is exactly where the road joins the loop. Floyd finds that spot in O(n) time and O(1) space without touching the array.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Compare every pair (i, j). The first equal pair is the duplicate.
approaches.why: Two nested loops: about n·n/2 comparisons. With n up to 10⁵ that's ~5·10⁹ checks, way too slow.

approaches.name: Cyclic sort
approaches.idea: Value v belongs at index v-1. Keep swapping each value into its home. The duplicate finds its home already taken, so it gets left at a wrong index. Scan for it.
approaches.why: Every swap puts one value in its final home, so there are at most n swaps. Every other step does i++, at most n times. Total ≤ 2n steps.
approaches.warn: Modifies nums. LC 287 says you must not change the array, so mention this and move to Floyd.

approaches.name: Floyd's cycle detection
approaches.idea: Phase 1: slow moves 1, fast moves 2 until they meet inside the loop. Phase 2: one pointer restarts at 0, both move 1 step; they meet at the loop's start, which is the duplicate.
approaches.why: Phase 1 ends within one lap after slow enters the loop (≤ n steps). Phase 2 takes exactly L steps (≤ n). Only a few int variables.

quiz.q: Why do both pointers start at index 0?
options: No value is 0, so nothing points to 0 and it can never be inside the loop
It's the fastest place to start

quiz.q: Where are slow and fast when phase 1 ends?
options: Somewhere inside the loop, usually not at its start

quiz.q: Why does phase 2 meet exactly at the loop's start?
options: L + x = k·C, so walking L steps from the meeting point finishes full laps and lands on the start
It's a coincidence for small arrays

quiz.q: Why is cyclic sort not the final answer for LC 287?
options: It modifies the array, which the problem forbids
It fails when the duplicate repeats many times
